articles.title: The floating scarecrow saving seabirds from fishing nets
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A bird-shaped kite and a floating scarecrow with spinning eyes reduced seabird deaths in Cornish fishing nets by up to 71 percent in a two-year trial. The devices cost relatively little, don’t require significant changes to how fishers work, and are already on the market. An estimated 95,000 diving […]
The post The floating scarecrow saving seabirds from fishing nets first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

A bird-shaped kite and a floating scarecrow with spinning eyes reduced seabird deaths in Cornish fishing nets by up to 71 percent in a two-year trial. The devices cost relatively little, don’t require significant changes to how fishers work, and are already on the market.

An estimated 95,000 diving birds drown in gillnets off European coasts every year, including razorbills and guillemots, whose North Atlantic populations have been declining. Gillnets hang vertically beneath the water’s surface, nearly invisible to diving birds, which swim straight into them and can’t get back up. It’s been a documented problem for decades, and until now the solutions available to fishers who wanted to do something about it have been thin.

One floats at the net, the other flies like a hawk

The looming-eyes buoy, developed by Fishtek Marine, floats at the surface above the net and has a spinning head with two large eyes. As it rotates in the water, the eyes create a visual deterrent right at the spot where diving birds typically enter. The bird-shaped kite flies from the stern and mimics a bird of prey, triggering the instinct diving birds have to steer clear of aerial predators.

Bycatch program manager Yann Rouxel of the RSPB called the results “a major milestone in the effort to reduce seabird bycatch without impeding gillnet fishers while at sea.” Conservation tools tend to fail in real-world adoption when they’re complicated, expensive, or get in the way of the work. A spinning buoy and a kite don’t fit that description.

Two years, ten Cornish fishers, and footage of every dive

Ten Cornish fishers partnered with Fishtek Marine and the RSPB, fitting cameras to their boats to monitor seabird behavior around the nets over two years. Scientists from the University of Exeter analyzed the footage and catch data. Their results, published in Conservation Letters, showed a 59 percent reduction in bycatch using the looming-eyes buoy and 71 percent using the kite. The study also identified that in Cornwall, most seabird bycatch happens in winter, which gives fishers and conservationists a seasonal window to concentrate device use rather than requiring year-round deployment.

“This study provides some of the strongest evidence to date that simple, practical deterrents can substantially reduce seabird bycatch in gillnet fisheries,” said lead author Tom Horton of the University of Exeter. “By also identifying when and where bycatch risk is highest, we now have a clear opportunity to target mitigation measures where they can deliver the greatest conservation benefit.”

What comes next

Both devices are commercially available, which cuts down the time between having good evidence and being able to act on it. The RSPB has been researching gillnet bycatch for more than a decade; this study gives that work a number to point to. What’s less certain is how quickly the devices reach fishers beyond the ten in the trial, and whether fishery regulators move toward requiring their use in high-risk seasons and areas.

Razorbills and guillemots aren’t in immediate danger of extinction, but their populations have declined, and 95,000 birds a year is a loss that doesn’t have to happen. The fishers who ran the trial are already using both devices. Whether that becomes a wider shift depends largely on what fisheries managers make of a study that gives them a pretty clear answer.

articles.title: This “golden tree” coral was too strange for any known family
articles.summary: A brilliant yellow coral discovered off Costa Rica proved so unusual that scientists had to create an entirely new family to classify it. The meter-tall colonies rise from seafloors covered in brittle stars, inspiring the Tolkien-inspired name Laurinque elenya, or “golden tree of the stars.” Advanced genetic analysis revealed that the coral belongs to a previously unknown evolutionary lineage.
articles.content:
Scientists surveying underwater mountains off Costa Rica have identified a remarkable new coral that is unlike any known coral family. Its genetic makeup and physical features were so distinctive that researchers created an entirely new family to classify it. The bright yellow coral, which has a branching, tree-like appearance, was discovered between 360 and 529 meters below the Pacific Ocean's surface. The findings are reported in the open-access journal ZooKeys.

Some colonies grow more than a meter tall. Researchers collected specimens using the remotely operated vehicle SuBastian during expeditions in 2019 and 2023 aboard the research vessels Falkor and Falkor (too), which are operated by the Schmidt Ocean Institute. The expeditions explored seamounts near Isla del Coco and along Costa Rica's Pacific margin.

A Golden Coral Among Fields of Stars

The coral was especially abundant on rocky outcrops where brittle stars covered nearly every available surface. Against this shimmering backdrop, the bright yellow branches appeared to rise from the seafloor like glowing trees surrounded by stars.

That unusual scene helped inspire the scientific name. The new genus, Laurinque, is derived from "Laurinquë," which means "golden tree" in Quenya, the Elvish language created by J.R.R. Tolkien for The Lord of the Rings and The Silmarillion. Researchers selected the name because of the coral's vivid yellow color and tree-like shape.

Its species name, elenya, means "stellar" or "of the stars" in Quenya. The name refers to the dense populations of brittle stars surrounding the coral colonies. Together, the genus and species names reflect what the researchers described as an almost mystical elvish landscape on the deep ocean floor.

DNA Reveals a New Coral Family

Determining where the coral fit on the evolutionary family tree proved far more complicated than expected. Scientists initially sequenced three genes commonly used to identify and classify corals. Instead of pointing toward the same group, each gene suggested a different and unrelated family.

Because those results were unusually inconsistent, the researchers used phylogenomics, a method that compares hundreds of genes at the same time. The broader genetic analysis finally clarified the coral's evolutionary position.

The results showed that the species does not belong to any previously recognized coral family. It represents a distinct evolutionary lineage that is most closely related to Eunicellidae, but its genetics and anatomy differ enough to justify the creation of a new family called Laurinqueidae. Researchers also established the new genus Laurinque specifically for the species.

Dr. Odalisca Breedy of the Universidad de Costa Rica (lead researcher on the study) said:

"I saw the octocoral garden for the first time in 2019 and I was impressed by the beauty of the landscape, which inspired, later the elvish name of the taxa. I thought the species could belong to a known family and genera, but after the preliminar morphological analysis I realised that it was something very different that I could not match with the known taxa.

"In 2023 we collected more samples and thanks to the exhaustive molecular analyses made by my colleagues, Cathy McFadden, Catalina Murillo and Andrea Quattrini, we were able to determine the taxonomic placement of the stunning species, in one of the most enigmatic sites."

Costa Rica's Deep Sea Still Holds Surprises

Dr. Breedy led the research with an international team of collaborators. The Schmidt Ocean Institute supported the expeditions, along with a National Geographic Society research grant.

The find joins a growing number of previously undocumented species discovered on Costa Rica's seamounts. It also highlights how much of the deep ocean remains poorly explored, even though it covers roughly two-thirds of Earth's surface.

Coral gardens like this one are considered vulnerable marine ecosystems. Their complex three-dimensional structures provide habitat for many other forms of deep-sea life, making them important centers of biodiversity in environments that scientists are only beginning to understand.
articles.reasoning: The discovery of a new coral species that required the creation of an entirely new family represents a significant scientific breakthrough with broad implications for marine biodiversity and conservation. It highlights the rich, unexplored biodiversity of deep ocean ecosystems, which are important vulnerable habitats supporting many species. The detailed genetic analysis and international collaboration add substance and significance to the story.

articles.title: Number of known species of giant waterlilies almost doubles
articles.summary: A new species of giant waterlily identified with the help of social media and satellite photos is just one of three discovered in the past few years
articles.content:
A new species of giant waterlily identified with the help of social media and satellite photos is just one of three discovered in the past few years

Victoria colombiana, a species of giant waterlilly now identified as a new species Carlos Magdalena

Giant waterlilies are not exactly inconspicuous plants. But in the past few years, we have discovered no fewer than three new species, taking the total to five. The latest species to be described was identified with the help of social media, satellite photos and a mad jungle dash in the dark.

“I think it’s incredible that we find something so new, which is so large, in this world where we think everything is already known,” says Maarten Christenhusz at the Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland, who has helped describe two of the new species.

Giant waterlilies are famed for their massive leaves, which grow up to 3 metres wide. For many decades, just two species were known: Victoria amazonica and Victoria cruziana. Then in 2016, Carlos Magdalena at the Royal Botanic Gardens in Kew, London, noticed that giant waterlilies grown from seeds from Bolivia were a bit different, with even larger leaves. In 2022, Magdalena and his colleagues published a paper showing that this was a new species, Victoria boliviana.

Advertisement

Magdalena hasn’t stopped there. In 2021, Jeremiah Harris, who runs a carnivorous plant business in the US, posted pictures online that he took while swimming near the Inírida river in Colombia next to what he assumed was V. amazonica.

Magdalena was struck by the photos because scientists had thought there were no giant waterlilies in this region. “This river is geographically completely separated from the Amazon, and has been for millions of years, and that is why this is such an interesting find,” says Christenhusz.

The power of science See Chris Packham at New Scientist Live 2026 Find out more

Magdalena, Christenhusz and their team examined satellite photos and found telltale green dots confirming there really were giant waterlilies growing there. They then organised an expedition to the region. The team found two plants but neither was flowering – and analysing the flowers is a crucial step in establishing whether a waterlily really is a new species.

At 11pm on the last night of the expedition, with the plane due to leave at 9am, the researchers seemed to have failed. Then one of the guides, Gustavo Melo from the Indigenous Tucano community, said he knew where some more giant waterlilies were growing. The team set off by boat in the dark, and found five plants in a small lake just before sunrise, including some that were flowering.

Magdalena, Christenhusz and their colleagues have now published a paper describing the new species, which they have named Victoria colombiana. It differs from V. amazonica in the orientation of the spines beneath the leaves, and in the shape of its flowers and fruits. The spines are a defence against manatees and plant-eating fish, Christenhusz says, so they vary between species depending on which herbivores are most prevalent.

As far as the team is aware, V. colombiana is found in only one small area. A single event, such as a pollution spill, could wipe out the entire species, says Christenhusz. But the team is planning to try to collect seeds to help ensure the species survives.

Meanwhile, Magdalena also realised that the giant waterlilies growing in the Pantanal region of South America, hundreds of kilometres to the south-east of Colombia, must have been isolated from other populations for a very long time. Sure enough, genetic studies revealed that they are another distinct species, despite looking very similar to V. cruziana. Magdalena, Christenhusz and their colleagues will publish a paper soon to describe this fifth species, which they have decided to name Victoria mattogrossensis.
articles.reasoning: The article reports the discovery of three new species of giant waterlilies, significantly expanding scientific knowledge of biodiversity. These discoveries were aided by innovative methods including social media and satellite imagery, and have broad significance for conservation and understanding of ecosystems. The story provides detailed context about the species, their habitats, and conservation concerns, highlighting a meaningful positive impact on environmental science and biodiversity preservation.

articles.personality_presentation_es:

Estos esfuerzos apoyan la conservación y fomentan el uso de nuevas tecnologías y conocimientos locales para descubrir y proteger la vida vegetal.

**Resumen en una frase** – Usando redes sociales, imágenes satelitales y guías locales, los científicos casi han duplicado las especies conocidas de nenúfares gigantes, ampliando nuestro conocimiento sobre la diversidad de plantas y la conservación.

articles.title: ‘Overshoot is not a reason to surrender’: UN calls for accelerated climate action ahead of COP31 summit
articles.summary: As world leaders prepare for November’s major COP31 climate summit in Türkiye, record-breaking heat, devastating floods and an unprecedented El Niño climate pattern are making global climate action ever more urgent.
articles.content:
Ahead of the summit, leaders gathered for a pre-conference in the South Pacific this week to prepare for the intense negotiations to come and set the agenda.

UN Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed joined senior government figures and top policy makers in Tuvalu and Fiji – two Pacific island nations facing the brunt of rising seas and intensifying floods – to lay out the UN’s climate priorities.

“We must take urgent action to ensure every child born today across the Pacific Islands can grow up, prosper and live on the islands they call home,” she told the pre-COP in Fiji.

‘Keeping 1.5 alive’

A key priority raised by the UN Deputy Secretary-General was “keeping 1.5 alive” – referencing the 2015 Paris Agreement target to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels.

As the world is heading to exceed the 1.5°C target, Ms Mohammed urged states not to give up.

“Overshoot is not a reason to surrender,” she said in Tuvalu. “It is a call to accelerate – to make overshoot as short and small as possible and bring temperatures back down below 1.5 as quickly as possible.”

Reduce emissions, boost security

She called on leaders to deliver on promises made at previous climate conferences, most notably the 2023 Climate Change Conference in Dubai (COP28) where leaders agreed to transition away from fossil fuels, triple renewable capacity and double energy efficiency by 2030.

She highlighted the benefits of this transition to renewables by linking it directly to energy security.

“For the 655 million people still living without electricity, clean power means a mother surviving birth with the lights on, and a child doing her homework after dark,” she said in Fiji.

“It frees economies from the price swings from impacts of global conflicts on fossil fuels.”

Protect and adapt

At the same time, with the impacts of global warming already being felt, the UN Deputy Secretary-General also called for stronger adaptation and protection measures.

© UNICEF/Lasse Bak Mejlvang

She urged countries to expand early warning systems, which help predict extreme weather events and alert communities before disaster strikes.

“An early warning that reaches a family hours before a cyclone gives them time to get to safety,” she explained in Fiji.

These systems must be complemented by resilient infrastructure, secure water supplies and healthy ecosystems, she stressed, highlighting ongoing efforts in Pacific communities to strengthen coastal resilience and restore marine ecosystems.

Fair funding

To enable this transition, a quick, fair and clear funding scheme is critical.

She reiterated that developed countries should take the lead – pointing to the Baku to Belém Roadmap which aims to mobilise at least $1.3 trillion annually in climate finance for developing countries by 2035.

Crucially, she emphasised that funding must be easy to access.

“Every dollar has to arrive where it is meant to go. A small island ministry with a handful of staff should be able to reach concessional finance quickly and simply,” she said in Fiji.

“The UN's message remains emphatic: Keep the promise of Paris, fight harder, and make the tragic overshoot as small and short as possible,” she emphasised.

articles.personality_title_fr: L’ONU appelle à une action climatique accélérée avant la COP31 pour protéger les îles vulnérables
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Face à la montée des températures, aux inondations et à un phénomène El Niño exceptionnel, les dirigeants mondiaux se préparent au sommet climatique COP31 en novembre en Turquie. Cette réunion vise à renforcer la lutte contre le changement climatique.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Cette semaine, des dirigeants se sont réunis dans le Pacifique Sud, dont la Vice-Secrétaire générale de l’ONU, Amina Mohammed, pour discuter des priorités climatiques. Ils étaient à Tuvalu et aux Fidji, deux nations insulaires gravement touchées par la montée des eaux et les inondations. Mme Mohammed a souligné l’importance de maintenir le réchauffement en dessous de 1,5 degré Celsius, un objectif clé de l’Accord de Paris de 2015.

**Impact** – L’ONU a insisté sur le fait que même si les températures dépassent temporairement 1,5 degré, les pays ne doivent pas abandonner mais agir plus vite pour réduire les émissions et faire baisser les températures. La transition vers les énergies renouvelables est aussi liée à une meilleure sécurité énergétique, ce qui peut aider des millions de personnes sans électricité. Les systèmes d’alerte précoce et des protections renforcées, comme des infrastructures résistantes et des écosystèmes sains, sont essentiels pour aider les communautés à survivre aux événements climatiques extrêmes.

**Prochaine étape** – L’ONU appelle les pays développés à fournir un financement équitable et facile d’accès pour aider les nations vulnérables à s’adapter et réduire leurs émissions. Les dirigeants à la COP31 chercheront à renforcer les engagements passés et à accélérer l’action pour limiter les dégâts climatiques.

**Résumé en une phrase** – L’ONU demande une action climatique plus rapide et un soutien équitable pour protéger les communautés vulnérables, notamment les îles du Pacifique, avant le sommet COP31.
articles.personality_title_es: ONU pide acelerar la acción climática antes de la COP31 para proteger a las islas vulnerables
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Ante el aumento de temperaturas, inundaciones y un fenómeno de El Niño inusual, los líderes mundiales se preparan para la cumbre climática COP31 en noviembre en Turquía. Esta reunión busca fortalecer los esfuerzos contra el cambio climático.

**Qué pasó** – Esta semana, líderes se reunieron en el Pacífico Sur, incluyendo a la Subsecretaria General de la ONU, Amina Mohammed, para discutir prioridades climáticas. Estuvieron en Tuvalu y Fiji, dos naciones insulares afectadas por la subida del nivel del mar y las inundaciones. Mohammed destacó la importancia de mantener el calentamiento global por debajo de 1,5 grados Celsius, objetivo clave del Acuerdo de París de 2015.

**Impacto** – La ONU insistió en que, aunque las temperaturas superen temporalmente los 1,5 grados, los países no deben rendirse sino acelerar la reducción de emisiones para bajar de nuevo la temperatura. La transición a energías renovables también mejora la seguridad energética, ayudando a millones que aún no tienen electricidad. Los sistemas de alerta temprana y protecciones fuertes, como infraestructuras resistentes y ecosistemas saludables, son vitales para que las comunidades sobrevivan eventos climáticos extremos.

**Próximo paso** – La ONU pide a los países desarrollados que proporcionen financiamiento justo y fácil de acceder para ayudar a naciones vulnerables a adaptarse y reducir emisiones. Los líderes en la COP31 buscarán avanzar en compromisos previos y acelerar la acción para limitar el daño climático.

**Frase clave** – La ONU insta a acelerar la acción climática y a brindar apoyo justo para proteger a las comunidades vulnerables, especialmente las islas del Pacífico, antes de la cumbre COP31.
